quarterly_data.signal: When industry supply actually arrives: 'We think that meaningful supply will start to ramp only in 2028. And that too, it'll be only an initial ramp. It'll gather momentum only in the years after. It will take a while for the industry to find a new equilibrium point. But when exactly that happens, we don't have line of sight to yet.' Because tech transitions no longer produce enough bit growth, the whole industry needs greenfield clean room space at the same time, which is gated by construction, permitting and infrastructure. Cycle-time context on why memory supply cannot respond quickly: roughly 2,000 process steps in the fab, three and a half plus months (approaching four months) through the fab plus a month - or a month and a half for more complex products - in assembly, packaging and test, so about a five-month cycle time from wafer start to customer shipment.

quarterly_data.signal: Custom HBM begins at HBM4E and HBM is becoming a one-to-two-supplier market. Asked when custom HBM can be material: 'HBM4E is when there is going to be a custom SKU of HBM as we work with customers on, and there is plenty of opportunity for differentiation in HBM.' Beyond the custom opportunity, the core design and qualification of HBM is so time-consuming, R&D-intensive and expensive that it is not practical for customers to do business with all three HBM suppliers for all projects: many projects, platforms and several customers will end up using ONE OR TWO HBM suppliers and only a very small number will use all three, so HBM becomes a two-supplier market and 'oftentimes, just a single-sourced opportunity.' On supply mix, the HBM-to-DDR trade ratio of 3-to-1 at HBM3E (to produce 100 bits of HBM, 300 bits of DDR supply must be given up) worsens to CLOSER TO 4 TO 1 by the time Micron reaches HBM4E.
quarterly_data.figure: custom HBM SKU starts with HBM4E; HBM3E-to-DDR trade ratio 3-to-1 worsening to closer to 4 to 1 at HBM4E; HBM a one-to-two-supplier market per platform

Supply growth stays structurally constrained: diminishing returns from technology transitions, HBM growing faster than conventional DRAM through 2028 (a rising share of industry output), higher trade ratios as the industry shifts from HBM3E to HBM4 and toward HBM4E late in 2027, and above all cleanroom space - even with first wafer output from Idaho mid-calendar 2027, meaningful supply growth takes a few quarters after a cleanroom opens. Bhatia: 'we really do not have line of sight to when supply and demand balances', and these are 'the reasons why we see that DRAM is reducing supply industry shipments next year'. About 3/4 of SCA revenue has a defined pricing framework and about 1/4 is open to periodic price negotiation with market dynamics; most pricing frameworks carry floor and ceiling bands, and the newer agreements are negotiated at current market conditions rather than the Q2 conditions of the earlier ones. quarterly_data.signal: MEMORY-RELATED NET SYSTEM SALES NOW GUIDED TO GROW OVER 75% IN 2026 — memory was 49% of Q2 net system sales (EUR 6.6B total). Driver per CEO Christophe Fouquet: 'the supply challenges driving up both DDR AND HBM PRICES have prompted significant investments in fab expansion', with customers adding meaningful capacity this year AND planning MULTIPLE MEGA FABS that come online in phases over the coming years. Growth is a combination of (1) much higher VOLUME for both HBM and DDR — 'HBM will require more wafer, there's a volume effect' — with some product mix shifting toward DDR on very strong DDR pricing, and (2) rising LITHO INTENSITY as customers migrate to advanced nodes: the 1c node ('going to be enormous') and 1b use more EUV layers, with Low-NA EUV growth driven by replacing multi-patterning with more cost-effective SINGLE-EXPOSE EUV, plus more immersion DUV. Fouquet: 'this combination which create a bit the perfect storm for ASML on DRAM this year and most probably the next few years to come.' Company-wide: Q2 net sales EUR 9.3B above guidance, FY2026 raised to EUR 43-45B; ~65 Low-NA EUV systems shipping in 2026 with 2027 Low-NA EUV nearly sold out and capacity being raised ~30%.

I will still pick mostly memory', because demand for high bandwidth memory (the AI memory) is extremely high and demand for DDR memory is also very high, so DRAM prices went up significantly in recent weeks. Memory customers are moving very aggressively because 'capacity is also market share'; 2026 memory demand 'will be very, very tight', and DRAM customers started building capacity as quickly as possible most probably at the end of last year. quarterly_data.signal: CEO: DRAM demand keeps rising, driven by AI, but capacity is limited by cleanroom space. Many customers are squeezing in an extra couple of tools, and large tool volumes will come only when the new fabs open. DRAM is expected to be significantly up in 2026 over a lower 2025 base, with momentum into 2027 across all DRAM manufacturers as the cleanroom bottleneck eases. As an example he cited SK hynix's Yongin cluster, '4 mega fabs of 200,000 wafer starts a week', where he expects SK hynix to start taking systems around early 2027 to ramp the fabs. DRAM prices are spiking because supply is very constrained.

quarterly_data.signal: Implant capital intensity: for DRAM, customers typically spend about $150 million to $200 million on implant equipment for every 100,000 wafer starts brought online. Axcelis already has a very good position in high energy and is building on its high current position, which is why management is positive on high current.

contracts.signal: Besi, with its hybrid bonding technology, together with Applied Materials in automated line concepts, is at the forefront of this technology being used in the memory; the company is working with Applied Materials on automated line concepts for memory applications as HBM evaluations proceed at the three memory makers

quarterly_data.signal: ALL THREE memory makers now have BESI hybrid bonders evaluating HBM stacking: the US memory customer placed REPEAT orders; the Korean customer (see Samsung's own website on HB for HBM) moved its 2-year lab program to the forefront with TWO applications (logic + HBM); and 2 evaluation tools shipped to the third memory maker (full tool-of-record evaluation). A VERY BIG END CUSTOMER has invited all three to have hybrid-bonded HBM stacks ready by END-2026 for use in 2027 end products - HBM4E is the insertion point. Timeline: 2026 = major qualification year (first customer aiming June/July, second end-Q3/Q4), production capability set up late 2026, MAINSTREAM VOLUME PRODUCTION 2027. TAM rule of thumb intact: ~150 HB systems for logic implies ~600 for HBM (a 16-high stack needs 16 bonds vs 1 for logic; each 2.5D module carries 3-4 stacks). For HBM high-volume production the integrated configuration (with Applied Materials Kinex automated lines) is the likely choice vs standalone for logic flexibility - bonder value to BESI is the same either way. JEDEC's possible 20-high stack height relaxation (775 -> 825/900um) does NOT change HB economics (only one of the three needs the extra height); interconnect yields must prove >99.9% (already 99.99%+ in logic HB).

quarterly_data.signal: DE-SPECCING DOES NOT DENT HBM PROCESS-CONTROL INTENSITY: asked about customer de-speccing (the analyst's framing - AI servers putting in less memory and stepping from 12 high to 8 high), Higgins argues 'the roadmap dynamics I talked about earlier, those are generally unchanged in the HBM environment' - redundancy, IO count, die size and performance specs still hold, and 'You cannot bin an HBM device'. He reads the behaviour as a reaction to today's memory pricing and supply-demand imbalance rather than a roadmap change, and says KLA does not like paying today's memory prices either. Supporting context he gave on intensity: HBM carries less redundancy, larger die and more logic-like attributes with more logic in the base die, 'the actual device only performs as good as the weakest DRAM in the device', and 'In some products, we have seen intensity in High-Bandwidth Memory that has been consistent with what we see in advanced logic.' Conventional memory is also improving for KLA, with more EUV layers in conventional DRAM devices than in the past.

Higgins added that with high-performance compute, customers can no longer bin devices, which drives more rigor to ensure 'each of the devices in the stacks' performs to tight specs; it also opens more service-contract penetration as customers keep tools at maximum uptime. Asked whether DRAM intensity could approach advanced logic, Wallace said it is 'still a ways away from advanced logic given the high mix of designs' and he was not ready to commit to that. KLA models the DRAM part of WFE up 15% to 20% in 2026, 'driven mostly by the demands for HBM'. quarterly_data.signal: HBM GROWTH DECOMPOSED, AND THE THIRD DRAM CUSTOMER OPENS UP. FormFactor's largest customer is the HBM leader, where it is the strong incumbent. At the third DRAM maker the major competitor is the entrenched incumbent and FormFactor sees less adoption of its high-speed stack-die configuration — but 'there is a very active conversation with that customer about what to plan for in 2027 and into 2028, as we have more capacity available to serve them'. On the HBM de-spec debate, Slessor called it 'much ado about nothing': fewer/simpler stacks would be offset by more HBM units and by more networking infrastructure to transact data across those units, leaving it 'net net... neutral'. He framed the whole test tailwind as a chiplet problem — in an HBM stack 'one of the 16 die actually causes the entire stack to be essentially scrapped and lost' without known-good-die certainty.

quarterly_data.signal: Product pipeline as described in the half-year report: (1) CUBE PROBER - HBM test equipment that fully inspects HBM at the individual-stack level with sub-5-micrometre vision precision, skipping the loader/unloader/COK tray steps by transferring wafers directly to the chuck; first Samsung HBM Cube Prober order won 2025-01 and a KRW 9,720M HBM test equipment supply contract with Samsung disclosed 2026-05-19; filing says the HBM market is led by SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron and that stacked-die (TSV) inspection difficulty is driving double-digit annual growth in memory ATE. (2) Probe stations TWP300 (in mass-production lines) and second-generation-vision TWP300H targeting localisation of a market dominated by Tokyo Electron and other Japanese vendors. (3) Burn-in chambers and sorters - started with overseas SSD burn-in, expanding to DRAM and non-memory; eSSD / PCIe 5.0-6.0 burn-in demand tied to AI data-center build-outs. (4) Memory, non-memory (SoC) and module/SSD test handlers plus change-over kits and interface boards sold as a handler-plus-board total solution. Filing frames test and inspection equipment as the fastest-growing equipment segment because HBM-style advanced packaging requires 100% inspection at each process step, raising both ASP and unit counts. Corporate: new Taiwan branch manager approved 2026-07-07; subsidiary CK Electronic Technology Nanjing liquidated in H1; charter amended 2026-03-24 to rename outside directors as independent directors and extend directors' duty of loyalty to shareholders; KRW 15,000M of capital surplus transferred to retained earnings.

Onto expects to ship MULTIPLE ATLAS G6 SYSTEMS TO A MAJOR DRAM CUSTOMER in H2 2026 to support next-generation memory devices - the first DRAM customers to adopt the platform, following the gate-all-around logic customers named last quarter. quarterly_data.signal: CFO: after a rather soft Q1, Q2 group revenue rose 20% quarter-over-quarter to almost EUR 66 million, an 8% increase year-over-year; Material Solutions +7% and Metrology +9%. H1 2026 revenue EUR 120 million, more or less at the H1 2025 level: Material Solutions EUR 67.6 million (10% below H1 2025; expected to turn around in H2 2026 based on the order book) and Metrology EUR 53 million (20% above H1 2025). CEO: Metrology is contributing a growing share of group revenue.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 revenue almost EUR 66 million (+20% QoQ, +8% YoY); H1 EUR 120 million; Material Solutions H1 EUR 67.6 million (-10%); Metrology H1 EUR 53 million (+20%)

quarterly_data.signal: CFO: gross profit margin was 30% in Q2, up from 28.5% in Q1 (29.3% for the first half because of the weak Q1). EBITDA fell from EUR 6.7 million in Q1 to EUR 3 million in Q2, hit by non-period expenses of a little less than EUR 4 million - the largest a provision for potential compensation with one customer in Material Solutions (CFO: an individual system on an old model, a one-off, not a structural issue, still under negotiation), plus a higher valuation of the 2023-2026 LTI program. Material Solutions margins are below where management wants them because large orders received in Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 are still in engineering and sourcing, leaving underutilization; Metrology gross margin is at the expected high level but its EBITDA is burdened by investments in sales / service infrastructure, higher R&D and free demo systems. An efficiency program in Material Solutions (redesigned operational processes, strategic purchasing, shorter lead times, new leadership structure) started as a pilot at one site; rollout starts in 2026 and the CEO expects the majority to be done within 2027.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 gross margin 30% (Q1 28.5%; H1 29.3%); EBITDA EUR 6.7 million (Q1) -> EUR 3 million (Q2); non-period expenses a little less than EUR 4 million

quarterly_data.signal: ORDER INTAKE: CEO says H1 2026 order intake rose by more than 80% year-on-year, supported by both segments; CFO: H1 orders EUR 89 million in Material Solutions and almost EUR 100 million in Metrology. Q2 order intake rose 13%: EUR 30 million in Material Solutions, including follow-up orders for compound materials like indium phosphide, and EUR 35 million in Metrology, a bit above the expected run rate of EUR 30 million (Q1 was exceptionally strong; Q2 a more normalized level). CFO expects H2 2026 order intake to stay at a solid level with project-driven volatility: Material Solutions on a very good level comparable to H1 (Q3 vs Q4 timing depends on contract closings), Metrology developing gradually over H2. CEO: Metrology orders now arrive step by step against customer forecasts rather than as one-off volume orders, with four to six months of lead time depending on the customer; demand comes from the North American and Asian markets, and the high-volume business significantly overachieved the manual / semi-automated system business this year (nearly 50/50 in 2025).
quarterly_data.figure: H1 order intake >80% YoY (Material Solutions EUR 89 million, Metrology almost EUR 100 million); Q2 order intake +13% (Material Solutions EUR 30 million, Metrology EUR 35 million vs EUR 30 million run rate)

quarterly_data.signal: GUIDANCE: management confirms full-year 2026 guidance for revenue and EBITDA, with EBITDA expected in the lower half of the guidance range. CFO expects Q3 revenue in the direction of Q2 and an acceleration in Q4 coming from the order book (large Material Solutions orders moving into production), a gradual gross margin increase, a Q3 EBITDA margin approaching double-digit levels again, H2 OpEx below H1 (no repeat of the non-period expenses), and the majority of 2026 capex in the second half. CFO on risk: the H2 plan rests mostly on the order book; risks are execution related, e.g. a customer deferring a delivery under point-in-time revenue recognition.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 guidance confirmed; EBITDA in lower half of range; Q3 revenue in the direction of Q2, Q4 acceleration; Q3 EBITDA margin approaching double-digit

quarterly_data.signal: METROLOGY CAPACITY FULL: CFO says the existing Metrology product lines are already at full capacity for H1 2027 and the production lines under construction are quickly filling up; first orders received for 2028. CEO: a capacity ramp-up goes live by year-end, giving higher capacity from 2027 that is already starting to fill; visibility extends over the next years, partly into 2029, and 2027 orders and forecasts show the planned lines will be filled well in 2027. Asked whether current capacity is closer to about EUR 100 million of annual sales with a significant step up towards year-end, the CEO answered 'Roughly.'
quarterly_data.figure: Metrology lines full for H1 2027; new capacity live by year-end; first orders for 2028; visibility partly into 2029; current capacity roughly EUR 100 million annual sales (CEO confirmation)

quarterly_data.signal: HBM / ACOUSTIC METROLOGY QUALIFICATION: CEO says the majority of the qualification processes discussed earlier are finalized and PVA TePla is in the volume business with those customers; it is qualified / in final agreements with half of the big logic and memory players and is working on the other half (his answer when asked about the second Korean memory player). Its ultrasound inspection is not tied to a process step such as hybrid bonding - it is important for 16-high stacks and future 3D structures. CEO expects such customers to use dual or sometimes triple sourcing, sees not much competition in the field today, and does not target being single source everywhere. Further customers include OSATs, with lower volume per customer than the big logic and memory players. CEO on co-packaged optics: relevant in certain aspects and beneficial for the business.
quarterly_data.figure: half of the big logic / memory players qualified or in final agreements; relevant for 16-high HBM stacks

quarterly_data.signal: INDIUM PHOSPHIDE FURNACES: CEO says AI is fueling demand for indium phosphide substrates for data-center communication and for PVA TePla's furnaces, with a shift from smaller wafers to larger six-inch wafers combined with a structurally tight supply. Internal base-case estimate: a rough volume of 500 to 600 furnaces over 2027 to 2030; because much competition comes from customers' internal designs, the addressable market is 20%-30% of the total, of which the CEO is 'very confident' to win a significant share. Price is a low one-digit million EUR amount per system depending on setup. First orders are in the books for execution in 2026 (very low volume, excluded from the forecast); the company is already in agreements with customers (not named) and existing capacity is sufficient as planned.
quarterly_data.figure: base case 500 to 600 furnaces over 2027-2030; addressable 20%-30%; low one-digit million EUR per system; six-inch wafers

quarterly_data.signal: OTHER MATERIALS AND OPTICAL METROLOGY: CEO says PVA TePla is primary partner in all major European aluminum nitride activities, moving from supplying R&D equipment to owning the process, for power electronics and UV photonics. Silicon carbide is a steady business with first discussions on 300 millimeter, which the CEO expects the market to adopt over the next few months; data centers drive SiC activity and automotive is picking up. In silicon, the CEO sees higher demand on capacity until 2027 with further investments in crystal-growing equipment contributing to mid-term volume targets. Optical metrology is being consolidated into PVA Vision with a center of excellence in Dresden (Coburg site closed), with a roadmap from front-end manual / semi-automated tools to automated back-end / packaging applications; CEO says none of the big players such as KLA sit in that market area.
quarterly_data.figure: aluminum nitride: primary partner in all major European activities; SiC: first discussions on 300 millimeter

quarterly_data.signal: AI / HBM / ADVANCED PACKAGING framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the company says the surge in AI semiconductor demand has raised the importance of HBM and advanced-packaging processes, pushing up the technical barrier for high-purity chemicals and precision polishing materials; the global semiconductor market is growing at an unprecedented pace on AI data-center memory and on-device AI, and the introduction of sub-2nm GAA processes and volume production of 300+ layer V-NAND are driving continued demand for high-performance etchants and next-generation precursors. Seasonality has flattened because AI and cloud enterprise demand now leads, producing a longer up-cycle. Product positioning: special etchants for sub-2nm GAA, next-generation CMP slurry and precursors for HBM4 stacking; ultra-high-purity chemicals supplied at near-exclusive levels to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix from the leading-edge ramp and ultra-high-layer V-NAND development stage; a completed portfolio of TSV formation and planarisation materials for HBM4 and chiplet structures to lift high-value-added revenue; display unit expanding into glass-substrate processing materials for next-generation packaging; customers' processes moving to GAA and to HBM / 400+ layer NAND, with joint development from the process-design stage. US entities Soulbrain TX LLC (2022) and Soulbrain RASA TX LLC (2024) respond in real time to customers' new fab lines in Texas and North America; the Xi'an entity supports China memory lines. Semiconductor material ASPs +5% vs FY2025 while raw-material costs rose +14%; semiconductor materials 85% of H1 revenue, +31% company-wide revenue growth.
